hub.description: Decks and fences in Smithville, TN, planned for steep Center Hill Lake lots, older yards near the square, and rural DeKalb County land.
hub.intro: Most Smithville homes sit in one of two settings. Some are in town, on older lots near the courthouse square, where the neighbors are close and privacy is the main concern. Others are out toward Center Hill Lake, on steep, wooded ground where the deck is often tall and faces the water. Either one can take a deck or a fence, but the planning is different for each. Below is what Smithville homeowners usually want to know before they ask for a price, with links to our deck and fence pages for more detail.

sections.heading: Lake lots on steep, wooded ground
paragraphs: Around Center Hill Lake, many houses were built into the hillside so the back of the house looks out over the water. The ground usually drops away fast behind them, so a deck off the main floor can end up far above the yard. Tall decks need longer posts and real bracing, and their footings often go into rocky ground. Getting lumber down a slope with trees in the way takes time too. All of that is why a lake deck near Smithville often costs more than a deck of the same size in town.

There is also a property question you do not get in town. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers manages Center Hill Lake, and on many lake lots the strip nearest the water is Corps land rather than yours. Private structures on that strip, including deck stairs, generally need Corps permission, and so does cutting trees there for a view. Our page for [deck building in Smithville](/deck-builder-smithville-tn/) covers tall deck framing, railings that keep the view open, and how to plan around the Corps.

sections.heading: Older yards near the courthouse square
paragraphs: Closer to Downtown Smithville, the questions change. Lots are smaller and flatter, and many of the houses are older. With neighbors that close, a privacy fence along the back and sides is what many people in town want first. Before any posts go in, find out where your property line really runs, because on an older lot it does not always follow the fence that is there now. Our [Smithville fence company page](/fence-company-smithville-tn/) covers surveys, pins, and privacy fence styles in more detail.

Decks in Smithville proper tend to be low and simple, often a platform off the back door with a short run of steps to the yard. Low does not mean trouble free, though. On an older house, the wall where the deck will be fastened needs a close look before anything is drawn, since a deck is only as solid as what it hangs on. The deck page explains what to check there and why airflow matters under a low deck.

sections.heading: Rural land around Smithville
paragraphs: A good part of DeKalb County is still farmland and wooded acreage, and plenty of Smithville homes sit on land well outside town. Out there, the first fence question is how much of the property you actually want to enclose, and the answer is usually far less than all of it. Gates should be wide enough for whatever you drive through them. A deck on a rural Smithville house is often simpler than one on a lake lot, but a long gravel drive or a soft yard can still decide how close a truck gets to the house.

sections.heading: Who to ask about permits and the Corps
paragraphs: Smithville has its own city limits, and many homes near the lake sit outside them in unincorporated DeKalb County. That decides who you call. Inside the city, start with Smithville City Hall. For homes beyond the city line, check with the county. Attached and raised decks need a permit in most places, and fence rules differ from one office to the next. Our guide on [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the general process, but the local office has the final word.

Many Smithville homes are not in an HOA, but some lake developments and newer subdivisions do have covenants. They often cover fence style and tree removal. If you have one, get approval in writing before work starts. For Smithville lake lots, the Corps is a separate question from both the city and any HOA, and it is worth asking before you plan anything near the shoreline.

sections.heading: Getting a price for a Smithville project
paragraphs: A few details make the first conversation about a Smithville deck or fence go faster. For a deck, tell us roughly how high the main floor sits above the ground behind the house and whether a truck can get close. On the fence side, know where your corners are or whether you have a recent survey. It also helps to know whether the lot is inside the Smithville city limits. When you have those answers, use the [estimate form](#estimate) on this page and tell us what you have in mind.

faqs.q: Can I build on the Corps land between my house and Center Hill Lake?
faqs.a: Plan on keeping any deck or fence on your own land. The Corps controls its shoreline property around the lake, and private structures there generally need its permission, which you should not assume you will get. Before you plan stairs or a fence near the water, find out where your line ends. Your survey should show it, and the Corps office that manages the lake can answer questions about its side.

faqs.q: Can you build a deck and a fence on the same Smithville property?
faqs.a: Yes, and planning both at once helps. The fence often needs to meet the deck, and the best gate location depends on where the stairs come down. On a lake lot, a small fenced area at the foot of the deck stairs gives a dog a safe spot without fencing the whole hillside. In town, a privacy fence can be laid out so it screens the deck from the house next door.

faqs.q: Why does a deck on a lake lot cost more than one in town?
faqs.a: Height is the biggest reason. A deck that sits high above a slope needs longer posts, more bracing, and longer stairs, and the footings often go into rock. Access adds to it, since materials may have to be carried down the hill by hand. Railings on a tall deck also take more thought, because they sit right in your view of the water. Most of that never comes up on a low deck in a flat Smithville yard.

deck.description: Deck builder in Smithville, TN for tall decks on steep Center Hill Lake lots and low decks in town. Plan posts, stairs, and railings first.
deck.intro: Many homes near Center Hill Lake are built into a hillside, with the main floor facing the water and the ground falling away behind it. A deck on that kind of house is often tall, and it is usually the main place to sit outside. Decks in town are a different job. They sit lower, and they are often attached to an older house with its own quirks. This page covers both kinds of Smithville deck, starting with hillside work because it raises the most questions.

sections.heading: Tall decks on Smithville lake lots
paragraphs: Height is what sets Smithville lake decks apart. When the main floor sits well above the slope, every post is long, and long posts need bracing so the deck does not sway when a crowd moves across it. The connection to the house matters just as much. A tall deck puts more strain on its ledger board than a low one, so the ledger has to be fastened into solid framing with the right hardware and flashed so water cannot get behind it. None of that is visible once the boards are down, which is why it is worth asking about.

Stairs are the other big piece. On a steep lot near Smithville, the run from the deck to the yard can be long, and it often needs a landing partway down. Where the stairs end matters as much as how they start. A bottom step on soft soil that washes out in a hard rain will settle and pull the stringers out of line. Plan for it to land on firm ground or a small pad.

sections.heading: Footings in rocky Smithville ground
paragraphs: In many spots around Smithville, limestone sits close to the surface, and on steep hillsides the soil is often thin. A post hole that hits rock partway down cannot always be dug deeper with ordinary tools. Sometimes the rock can serve as the base, if the inspector agrees. Other times the footing has to shift over or change shape. Depending on where you live, the codes office may want to see footings before they are covered. When you compare deck builders around Smithville, ask each one how they handle rock. Call Tennessee 811 before any digging so buried utility lines get marked.

sections.heading: Where your land ends at Center Hill Lake
paragraphs: The Corps of Engineers manages Center Hill Lake, and on many lots the land nearest the water belongs to the Corps, not to the homeowner. Private structures there generally need Corps permission, so plan on keeping the deck on your side of that line. That sounds simple until you want stairs that reach toward the water or a lower platform partway down the hill. Before you design either one, find your line on a survey and ask the Corps office that manages the lake what it allows on its side.

Trees are the other catch. Plenty of Smithville lake owners want a clearer view from the deck, and the trees in the way are sometimes on Corps land. Cutting or trimming there is up to the Corps, not you. On your own land, check any HOA rules first, and think twice before removing healthy trees on a steep slope. Their roots help hold the hillside in place, and a bare slope under a deck can start to wash.

sections.heading: Railings that keep the lake in view
paragraphs: On a tall deck, the railing sits right in your line of sight when you look out at the water. Wood balusters are sturdy and usually cost less, but they block more of the view. Metal balusters and cable rail are easier to see through. Whatever you choose, the railing should meet whatever guard rules your codes office enforces for height and opening size, and on a tall deck it has to hold up to people leaning on it. Ask any Smithville deck builder you talk with how the railing posts are fastened to the framing, not just how the railing looks.

sections.heading: Using the space under a high deck
paragraphs: A tall deck leaves a lot of room underneath, and on a wooded lake lot outside Smithville that space is often shaded most of the day. Some owners want a patio there. Others want a dry place to keep kayaks and life jackets. Either way, water is the problem to solve. Rain falls through the gaps between boards, and on a slope it also runs downhill under the deck. If you plan to use that space, say so early, because it changes how the deck is built and where the water goes. You can note it on the [estimate form](#estimate).

sections.heading: Town decks and weekend houses in Smithville
paragraphs: Closer to Downtown Smithville, most decks are low platforms off a back door. They are simpler to build, but older houses bring their own questions. The siding may need to come off where the ledger goes, and the door threshold may sit at a height that makes the step out awkward. Check the band board behind the siding for rot before anything is attached to it. On a low deck, airflow under the framing matters too, since damp ground with little air moving is hard on wood.

Some lake houses around Smithville are weekend places or rentals. When you are not there every week, low upkeep counts for more, and the railings and stairs have to stand up to guests who do not know the house. Composite boards usually cost more at the start but skip the regular staining that wood needs. Under heavy tree cover, both still need cleaning to keep mildew off. Our guide to [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) lays out the tradeoffs.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Smithville?
faqs.a: A raised deck attached to the house needs a permit in most places, but who issues it depends on where the house sits. Inside the Smithville city limits, start with the city. Many lake homes are in unincorporated DeKalb County, so the county is the place to ask for those. Requirements can differ between the two, so confirm before work starts. HOA approval, if you have an HOA, is a separate step.

faqs.q: Is there a limit to how tall a deck on a lake lot can be?
faqs.a: There is no single answer. Your codes office sets the rules for your address, and a very tall deck may need drawings from an engineer before a permit is issued. What is certain is that height changes the build. The taller the deck, the heavier the posts and bracing need to be, and the longer the stairs get. If your main floor sits high above the slope near Smithville, mention it when you ask for a price.

faqs.q: What if a truck can't get close to where the deck goes?
faqs.a: That is common on lake lots near Smithville. Lumber and concrete may have to be carried down a slope by hand or moved in small loads, which adds labor. Tell us about access up front, including steep gravel drives and spots where a trailer cannot turn around. Access is one of the bigger reasons two decks of the same size can come in at very different prices.

faqs.q: How do I know if the old deck on our lake house is safe?
faqs.a: Start where the deck meets the house. Rot at the ledger, loose or rusted fasteners, and posts sitting in wet soil are the warning signs that matter most on a tall deck. Soft boards and wobbly railings are easier to spot. If the deck bounces or sways when people walk across it, have it checked before the next busy weekend. Our guide on [signs you need a new deck](/guides/signs-you-need-a-new-deck/) walks through what to look for.

faqs.q: Can a lower landing or second level be added on a hillside?
faqs.a: Often, yes, as long as everything stays on your land. A lower landing partway down the hill breaks up a long stair run and gives you a second place to sit. Anything that reaches toward the water runs into the Corps line on many lots, so check the survey first. Slope and rock both change what a second level costs, so it is usually cheaper to plan it with the main deck than to add it years later.

fence.description: Fence company in Smithville, TN for privacy fences near the square, dog yards on steep lake lots, and fencing on rural DeKalb County land.
fence.intro: Fence questions in Smithville depend a lot on where you live. In town, near the courthouse square, most people want privacy from a neighbor who is close by. Lake lots are a different story. The ground there is steep and wooded, and the goal is more often a safe spot for a dog than a fence around everything. Rural land in DeKalb County brings long runs and wide gates. This page walks through fence installation in each setting, along with the local questions worth answering before you hire a fence company.

sections.heading: Privacy fences near downtown Smithville
paragraphs: Lots near the square in Smithville are often older and closer together, which is why a privacy fence tends to top the list in town. Board on board and shadowbox styles are popular for this because both look finished from either side. On older lots, though, the fence line you inherited may not be the property line. Corner pins can be missing or buried, and an old chain link fence may have gone up wherever was easiest at the time.

Before new posts go in, it pays to know where the line actually is. A recent survey is the cleanest answer. If you do not have one, a surveyor can find or reset the pins. Talk with the neighbor early, especially if an old fence is coming out or a tree sits right on the line. Our guide on [fences and property lines](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) covers the general steps, including calling Tennessee 811.

sections.heading: Fencing a steep lot near Center Hill Lake
paragraphs: Lake lots around Smithville rarely have a flat yard to fence. The ground often drops off behind the house, and trees and rock break up any straight run. On slopes like that, panels can be stepped, so each section sits level and drops at the post, or racked, so the rails follow the grade. Stepped panels leave triangle gaps at the bottom that a small dog can slip through. Racked panels hug the ground more closely but work best on a steady slope. Our guide to [fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) explains both.

Most Smithville lake owners are not trying to enclose the whole hillside. A fenced area off the bottom of the deck stairs, or around a flatter patch near the house, is often enough for a dog. The fence also has to stop at your property line. On many lots, the land toward the water belongs to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and private fences there generally need its permission. Check your survey before you pick a layout.

sections.heading: Rocky ground and post holes in Smithville
paragraphs: In many spots around Smithville, limestone sits close to the surface, and a post hole can hit rock before it reaches full depth. Rock does not end a fence installation, but it changes the work. The hole may need to be drilled into the rock itself. In other spots, moving a post a short distance finds better ground. Either way it takes longer than digging in plain clay, and an honest estimate should account for it. On rural land, keep in mind that Tennessee 811 usually does not mark private lines, such as one running to a well or a barn.

sections.heading: Fence installation on rural acreage
paragraphs: Plenty of Smithville homes sit on several acres, and fencing all of it is rarely the plan. The usual goal is a fenced yard near the house for dogs or kids, with a gate wide enough for a riding mower. Some owners add a privacy fence along one side to screen a road or a neighbor's shop. Long runs over uneven ground need careful layout so the line stays straight and the posts stay plumb through every dip and rise.

If deer are the reason you want a fence, say so up front. An ordinary yard fence does not always keep them out of a garden, and a fence meant to stop deer is built differently from one meant to keep a dog in. Horses or cattle on the property are worth mentioning as well, since animals that lean on a fence call for a different design than a backyard fence.

sections.heading: Wood for shaded, humid yards
paragraphs: Many Smithville yards, especially near the lake, sit under a heavy tree canopy. Shade and humidity keep wood damp longer, which invites mildew and speeds up rot at the base of posts. Pressure treated pine is the common choice for posts because it is treated to resist rot in the ground. Cedar pickets look good and tend to stay straighter, but they cost more. On a shaded lot, how the posts are set and the gap left under the pickets matter as much as the choice of wood. Our guide on [cedar vs pressure treated](/guides/cedar-vs-pressure-treated-fence/) compares them.

sections.heading: Permits and HOA rules in Smithville
paragraphs: Fence rules vary from place to place. Inside the Smithville city limits, ask the city whether your fence needs a permit and whether there are limits near the street or on corner lots. Outside the city, check with DeKalb County. Many Smithville homes have no HOA, but some newer subdivisions and lake communities have covenants that set style and height. Get that approval in writing first. Many homeowners face the finished side toward the neighbor as a courtesy, and some covenants require it. Once those answers are in hand, the [estimate form](#estimate) is the next step.

faqs.q: Do I need a survey before putting up a fence in Smithville?
faqs.a: You do not always need a new one, but you do need to know where your line is. On older lots near downtown Smithville and on rural tracts, pins can be missing, and an old fence proves nothing about the line. If there is any doubt, a survey usually costs less than moving a fence later or settling a dispute with a neighbor. Keep a copy handy for any HOA or permit paperwork too.

faqs.q: Can I fence my lake lot all the way down to the water?
faqs.a: On many Center Hill Lake lots, no. The land nearest the water is often Corps property, and the fence has to stop at your line. Private structures on Corps land generally need the Corps' permission, so do not assume. If you want your dog to reach the water, that is a question for the Corps office that manages the lake, not for a fence company. A fenced area near the house that uses your side well is usually the practical plan.

faqs.q: Is a privacy fence worth it on a lake house we rent out?
faqs.a: It can be, especially if your Smithville rental allows dogs. A fenced area near the house gives guests a safe place to let a dog out, and a privacy fence can screen a hot tub or patio from the neighbors. Pick materials that need little care, since you may not be there to check on them often. Also look into any rules that apply to rentals where your property sits.

faqs.q: Can a fence go around trees instead of cutting them down?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The fence can jog around a trunk, or a post can be set a little away from the tree so fewer roots get cut. Leave some room for the trunk to grow. On a slope, roots are part of what holds the soil, so it is worth working around healthy trees when you can. Dead or leaning trees near the line are a different matter and are better dealt with before the fence goes in.

faqs.q: How close to the road can a fence go in Smithville?
faqs.a: That depends on where you are, and it is not something to guess. Inside the city, ask Smithville about setbacks and sight lines on corner lots. Along county roads, the right of way can extend well past the edge of the pavement, so the ditch line may not be yours to fence. Your survey should show it. An HOA may add its own rules on top of that.
